title: Pandanus

names.note: Also glossed 'pandanus palm'. Jajikal is also the name of the lower camp at Ayton, 'where there are lots of pandanus trees', and of the north side of the Bloomfield River mouth.

scientificName: Pandanus spiralis (as identified by Anderson 1996); the beach pandan is Pandanus tectorius

identification.basis: The dictionary glosses jajikal 'pandanus tree (screw palm)', and Anderson (1996, Table 2) identifies the Bloomfield jajikal as Pandanus spiralis. Current botanical keys call the pandanus of this coast's beaches and dunes P. tectorius, so the species name for the beach trees may need checking with botanists; Roth's Bloomfield name for the fruit, jillenji, does not match jajikal and is unexplained.

summary: **[Jajikal](word:jajikal)** is the pandanus or screw palm [ref:hershberger1982], the spiky, prop-rooted tree of the beaches and creek banks. Its name is written into the country: the lower camp at Ayton, 'where there are lots of pandanus trees', is called Jajikal, and the dictionary also gives Jajikal for the north side of the Bloomfield River mouth [ref:hershberger1982]. At Bloomfield the fruit was baked in the ashes and the hard shell broken to get at the seeds [ref:anderson1996]. Roth recorded that ripe fruit was sucked, while fruit not fully ripe had to be roasted first because raw it was too 'hot' [ref:roth1901]. The leaves were split for armlets, plaited work and toys [ref:roth1901-string] [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
The dictionary gives **[jajikal](word:jajikal)**, 'pandanus tree (screw palm)' and 'pandanus palm' [ref:hershberger1982]. It records the word as a place name too: the 'name of lower (bottom) camp in Ayton where there are lots of pandanus trees', and the 'north side of Bloomfield River mouth' [ref:hershberger1982]. Anderson's table of Bloomfield nut foods lists jajikal as *Pandanus spiralis* [ref:anderson1996].

Roth's 1901 list gives a different Bloomfield word, *jillenji*, for the pandanus **fruit**, and *na-rarl* from the Koko-yellanji at Butcher's Hill [ref:roth1901]. Neither matches jajikal, and *jillenji* looks more like the dictionary's *[jilanji](word:jilanji)*, an [edible fig](entry:fig). Whether Roth's informant mixed them up, or used a word for the fruit alone, is a question for Elders.

sections.heading: Description
sections.body: The beach pandan (*Pandanus tectorius*) grows to about 12 m, with a branched trunk studded with spiny, wart-like knobs and stilt-like **prop roots** up to 1 m long, themselves armed with short sharp points [ref:rfk-pandanus]. The long, strap-like leaves are up to 1.7 m long and 5–10 cm wide; the margins carry spines from just above the base to the tip [ref:rfk-pandanus]. The fruit is a big yellow or orange head, about 12–18 cm long, built from many hard, wedge-shaped segments, each about 4–5 cm long [ref:rfk-pandanus].

sections.heading: Where it grows
sections.body:
The beach pandan grows from sea level to 300 m in littoral rainforest, on sand dunes and coastal sandy country and in vine forest, from Cape York to central New South Wales [ref:rfk-pandanus].

Inland, pandanus lines creeks and rivers: *Pandanus spiralis* grows in 'savannah woodlands and poorly drained areas', on 'sand, alluvium and clay', across northern Queensland, the Northern Territory and the far north of Western Australia [ref:wp-spiralis]. Which pandanus grows where is set out under each place above.

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
**Food.** Roth's general entry for pandanus, which carries a Bloomfield name, says the fruit is sucked, the shell broken and the seed eaten, and that the roasted fruit can be soaked to make a sweet drink [ref:roth1901].

**Leaves.** Across North Queensland, Roth found pandanus leaves split for armlets (plain or plaited), plait-work, [dilly-bag](entry:dilly-bags) handles and sieve-bags, and used to smooth the gum-cement on [spear](entry:spear-and-woomera) barbs at Cooktown [ref:roth1901-string]. The pandanus-strip armlet was worn as far south on the east coast as the Bloomfield River [ref:roth1910-decoration], and Anderson confirms that Bloomfield people wore pandanus-leaf armlets [ref:anderson1996]. Children made small toy boomerangs from pandanus leaves [ref:anderson1996], and pandanus leaves made the little trough that fed water into the [zamia](entry:zamia) flour during leaching [ref:anderson1996].

**Building.** North of the Palmer River, Roth saw [huts](entry:huts-and-shelters) built on a ridge-pole held up by forked uprights, 'very commonly of Pandanus, the dichotomous growth of which lends itself admirably for the purpose' [ref:roth1910-huts].

sections.heading: How it was prepared
sections.body:
**Eating the fruit** — from Roth's pandanus entry [ref:roth1901] and Anderson's Bloomfield table [ref:anderson1996]:

1. **Collect** the fruit segments from a ripe yellow-orange head.
2. If the fruit is **very ripe**, suck the soft base of each segment raw.
3. If it is **not fully ripe**, roast or bake the segments in the **ashes** first. Raw, unripe fruit is too 'hot' to suck.
4. For a **sweet drink**, soak the roasted segments in water. The water becomes sweet and is drunk.
5. **Break the hard shell** and eat the seeds inside. In the Princess Charlotte Bay hinterland and on the Palmer River, Roth saw a hafted [stone](entry:stone) hammer used to break open hard nuts such as pandanus [ref:roth1904].

**Making a simple leaf armlet** — Roth's description from Cape Bedford and the Palmer district [ref:roth1901-string]:

1. Cut a strip of pandanus leaf, square at one end and tapering obliquely to a narrow end at the other.
2. Split the narrow end into four, six or more tags, all to the same depth.
3. Roll the square end around the hand two or three times and slip the coil off, holding it between thumb and forefinger.
4. With a sharpened stick, pierce small holes through the layers, one for each tag.
5. Pull each tag through its hole, knot the tags underneath in pairs, and trim the ends.

Roth adds that people sometimes just tied the ends instead [ref:roth1910-decoration].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body: Pandanus is well armed: the leaf margins carry sharp spines, and even the prop roots are studded with short sharp points [ref:rfk-pandanus]. Handle the leaves with care. Fruit that is not fully ripe is too 'hot' to suck raw, which is why it was roasted first [ref:roth1901]. The seed cases are very hard and were broken with [stones](entry:stone) [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Pandanus is not listed as threatened; as native plants the pandanus species here are 'least concern' wildlife under Queensland's Nature Conservation Act [ref:qld-plants-reg]. Under section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993*, native title holders do not need a licence or permit to hunt, fish or gather for their personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs [ref:alrc]. Everyone else needs the Traditional Owners' permission to take anything from country, and park rules apply: see each place above for whose country it is.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: Related words: *[jalngkal](word:jalngkal)* 'to remove a hard or tough covering, e.g. a coconut'; *[dalkil](word:dalkil)* 'to crack a nut'; *[jangka](word:jangka)* '[stone](entry:stone)'; *[dindal](word:dindal)* 'to roast on coals'; *[munja-l](word:munja-l)* 'to gather, collect (e.g. nuts, plant food)' [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: Pandanus grows in the Hann's country. The Atlas of Living Australia holds 38 pandanus records, from 1970 to 2024, in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru: most are *Pandanus cookii*, with a few of the inland *P. spiralis* [ref:ala-hann-pandanus]. No pandanus use is published for the Hann itself; the nearest records are Roth's, from the Princess Charlotte Bay hinterland the river drains into, and from Musgrave [ref:roth1904] [ref:roth1901-string].

sections.heading: Where it grows here
sections.body: *Pandanus cookii* is 'endemic to coastal and sub-coastal parts of tropical Queensland' and grows to about 10 m [ref:wp-cookii]; it is 24 of the 38 Atlas records in the Hann box. *P. spiralis*, with 5 records, grows in 'savannah woodlands and poorly drained areas' [ref:wp-spiralis]. The box holds a single record of the beach pandan, *P. tectorius*, the tree of the Bloomfield beaches [ref:ala-hann-pandanus] [ref:rfk-pandanus].

sections.heading: How people used it here
sections.body:
These records are Roth's, from about 1900, labelled by place:

- **The fruit.** Roth's pandanus entry, the fruit 'sucked, shell broken, and seed eaten', gives the names of two Princess Charlotte Bay peoples: Koko-rarmul *a-rárla* and Koko-warra *arú-ol* [ref:roth1901].
- **The hammer.** A hafted stone hammer was used 'for breaking open some of the harder nuts, e.g., pandanus'. Roth wrote: 'I found the implement in use throughout the Princess Charlotte Bay hinterland, in 1898' [ref:roth1904].
- **The leaves.** Pandanus leaves were split 'for plaitwork (Musgrave, Cape Bedford, etc.)' [ref:roth1901-string]. Musgrave Station is in today's Thaypan determination area [ref:fca-thaypan]. At Princess Charlotte Bay the women, 'and especially the younger girls', wore a necklace, *al-würa*, 'formed of strips of Pandanus leaf worked into a plait of from three to five strands'. The Koko-warra name for the pandanus-strip armlet was *raual* [ref:roth1910-decoration].
- **The frame.** North of the Palmer, which takes in the Hann, ridge-pole huts stood on forked uprights 'very commonly of Pandanus' [ref:roth1910-huts].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: The upper Hann is the Possum People's country [ref:fca-possum]; the middle and lower Hann are in the Thaypan native title determination of November 2023, held by the Awu-Laya Indigenous Corporation [ref:fca-thaypan]. Downstream, Rinyirru is jointly managed by the Rinyirru Aboriginal Corporation and the Queensland Government [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. Ask them before taking fruit or leaves.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: In Kuku Thaypan, the language of the middle and lower Hann, the pandanus (*Pandanus spiralis*) is **arral** [ref:hgdb-pandanus]. Roth's Princess Charlotte Bay names are under 'How people used it here'.

locations.summary: Pandanus is part of **Western Yalanji** country too: the inland *Pandanus spiralis* is recorded at Mount Carbine, and Edward Palmer reported pandanus fruit as a food on the Mitchell and Palmer rivers [ref:ala-pandanus] [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Where it grows here
sections.body: Inland, pandanus lines the creeks and rivers. The Queensland WildNet database records *Pandanus spiralis* at Mount Carbine [ref:ala-pandanus]; Roth recorded a Koko-yellanji name for pandanus at Butcher's Hill, inland [ref:roth1901]; and Edward Palmer, quoted by Roth, reported pandanus fruit as a food on the Mitchell and Palmer Rivers [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Uses here
sections.body: On the Middle Palmer, Roth found pandanus leaves split for sieve-bags [ref:roth1901-string], and the Koko-minni there called the plant, and the pandanus-strip armlet made from it, *anjoana* [ref:roth1910-decoration]. He saw the stone hammer that breaks open pandanus nuts in use on the Palmer in 1899 [ref:roth1904].

locations.summary: On Eastern Kuku Yalanji country jajikal is the beach pandan of Ayton, the Bloomfield mouth and the coves where people kept their permanent camps [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Uses here
sections.body: At Bloomfield, jajikal fruit was baked in the ashes and the shell broken first to get at the seeds; unlike many nuts it needed no pounding or [leaching](entry:leaching) [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: Much of Eastern Kuku Yalanji country is now Aboriginal land. On 29 September 2021 more than 160,000 ha, taking in the Daintree, Ngalba-bulal, Kalkajaka and Hope Islands national parks between Mossman and Cooktown, was handed back to the Eastern Kuku Yalanji people, to be jointly managed with the Queensland Government through the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service [ref:ag2021].
